maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. W. EDWARDS

speechtext:
Right Hon. WT. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, it is seldom that this House of Commons has witnessed a more sudden passing of one of its members than that which has taken from our midst the Honourable Dr. J. W. Edwards, member for Frontenac-Addington. Not twenty-four hours ago, honourable members on all sides of the house were glad to have the opportunity of expressing their pleasure at Dr. Edwards' return to his accustomed seat in this chamber, after an absence of but a day or two, occasioned by what at the time was regarded by many as a severe though not serious indisposition. It is now but too evident that Dr. Edwards must have known, even on Monday last, that his days were numbered. In the circumstances his coming back into the house yesterday afternoon was but one more example of great personal courage and of a sense of public duty which were characteristic o>f the whole of his public life.
That the House of Commons has been deeply touched by the death of one who has had a long association with its affairs, was apparent this morning when, despite the lack of opportunity of having public intimation made of the funeral service which was held in the forenoon, most of the members of this house, and, I venture to say, all who were aware of the service, were present in person to pay their last tribute of respect to his memory. That tribute, and the one which was paid by his fellow-members yesterday, is much more real and adequate than anything which it would be possible to express in words.
At the same time, I may, perhaps, be permitted, speaking more particularly for those of us who sit on this side of the house, to say how much we, in common with hon. members opposite, feel the loss which our country has sustained in the death of one who, though still in his sixty-fourth year, had had a long career of public service, in the course of
1674	. COMMONS
The late Hon. J. W. Edwards
which recognition of his abilities found expression in his appointment as a minister of the crown.
As one who was a graduate in arts and medicine of one of our leading Canadian universities, and who 'had followed the profession of teaching as well as that of a physician, Dr. Edwards with his native ability was well qualified to take an important part in the public life of this country. That those who knew him best were of this view is evidenced by his return to parliament in 1911, 1917, and 1925 and 1926, and by his appointment as a minister of the crown in 1921, to which I have just referred. We who were his fellow members in the House of Commons also shared that knowledge.
I confess that those of us who sat immediately opposite to our late friend felt, at times, that some of his criticisms and censures were unduly severe ; that they proceeded from a sincere motive and from an undaunted courage, none of us doubted.
There was, however, another side to the doctor's nature which was apparent to us all, and by which I am sure he would most wish to be remembered; it was his wide knowledge of public affairs, his ability and fearlessness as a public speaker, and, above all else, a great faithfulness in the discharge of his public duties as a member of parliament.
While his loss to the commons will be great, it will be particularly felt by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I detsire, on behalf of the members of the government to extend to my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition and to those who sit about him, our sincerest sympathy in the loss which he and the Conservative party have sustained in the passing of one of its foremost members.
There is one other expression of sympathy which I know all hon. members will wish to have made at this time, and which perhaps you, Mr. Speaker, will be kind enough to convey, and that is a mesage of profound sympathy to Mrs. Edwards and to her son and daughters in their overwhelming bereavement. I am sure few things we have witnessed have touched any of us more than the constant devotion, one to the other, of Dr. and Mrs. Edwards. Through all the storm and stress of his political life she was an ever faithful companion. I can see them now as they walked together toward these parliament buildings but a day or two ago, and I shall always recall the kindly smile which greeted me as we passed.
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]
It was that greater mellowness which came with years and which helped to reveal in increasing measure a keen sense of humour and a genuine kindliness of heart that won for Dr. Edwards the place which he had in the esteem and regard of members of this house. It will be remembered more and more as we leave behind the harsher aspects of the conflicts of party debate which, after all, are but of the day.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. W. EDWARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the very touching tribute which the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has paid to our fellow' member is greatly apreciated by those who sit to your left. Doctor Edwards was our colleague, and perhaps we who were more intimately associated with him better understood his nature and appreciated his merits, but the observations of the Prime Minister leave no room for doubt that in this house he had made the influence of his personality strongly felt, and as the yeaTs passed, his true wTorth was but the better recognized. We mourn Doctor Edwards as one of the stalwarts of our party, one whose exposition of the principles of the party with which he was associated was at all times given with conviction, with earnestness and sincerity, and for that reason our grief is more than mere passing sorrow.
While we have lost a great party leader and might say with one of old, "A Mighty Prince has this day fallen in Israel," the loss to his constituents and to his country must not be under-estimated. No constituency was more loyally or more faithfully served by the member representing it in this house than the constituency represented by Doctor Edwards. His profession enabled him to have a very singular hold upon the affections of his constituents, for every medical man who is a member of the house realizes that he has a great advantage in being able to speak to bis constituents in terms denied to many others of us. That Doctor Edwards was greatly beloved by those he represented many of us have reason to know, for we have seen manifestations of their affection in more ways than one.
While the loss to our party and to his constituents is great, I feel that the loss to this Dominion is greater still. I know of no man who had a greater love and affection for his country and a more real devotion to its well-being than Doctor Edwards. He had a firm faith and a profound conviction that

The late Hon. J. W. Edwards
this country was destined to play a very great part, among the peoples of the world. He yielded to no man in his confident faith and belief that our true destiny was to be found within the empire of which he was so devoted a servant, and at all times, whatever might be the matter engaging his attention, he made reference to that fact.
I think you will agree with me, sir, when I say that in losing Doctor Edwards we have lost a great member of parliament. I cannot recall of whom that observation was made, but certain it is that it was made with respect to one who about two centuries ago played a great part in the parliamentary history of England. Doctor Edwards was a great House of Commons man.	He believed in our
traditions. He had faith in representative government; he 'believed in the institutions of parliament, and respected and revered them. He had regard for forms, not for form's sake, but because he believed as most of us do, that in the maintenance of those forms we have the best guarantee for the preservation of the institution which we call parliament.
Then there was that side of his life which was so little known to many of us until we knew him more intimately-he was a great friend. His loyalty to his party was known to all, but his devotion to his friends was little understood. He was honoured by thousands of his fellow-Canadians by being placed in a position of very great authority in a powerful organization in this country, and yet I recall his saying to me that no man could point to a single observation that he had ever made in which he attacked any man's religion or denied to any one of his fellow-citizens the right to worship his own God under his own vine and fig tree. He had that tolerance which sometimes was denied to him. He had it to a singular degree. His love for his friends was very strong, and in this House of Commons, though sometimes his courage and the strength of his convictions found expression in terms that some of our friends took exception to, yet upon analysis, stripped of the surroundings under which the words were uttered, I think few could find cause for complaint or for just criticism.
We have indeed lost a friend, loyal, devoted and faithful friend, one whose service to his country cannot be measured by the accumulation of material possessions, but who has left behind him by his example and by the magnificent addresses which he delivered from
the Atlantic to the Pacific a feeling of faith in his country, based upon a stalwart Cana-dianism, coupled with a firm belief in the destiny of our empire and of this Dominion. These things will not easily nor soon be forgotten and as the years pass on I am satisfied that the feeling which was manifested yesterday when he returned to this House will be recalled as indicating the true measure of esteem and regard in which he was held by his fellow members. I recall, as the Prime Minister has mentioned, the words he spoke to me in the hospital only two days ago, and his appreciation of the manifestation of interest in his well-being shown by those whom he regarded as his political opponents, their inquiries as to his health and the hopes they expressed for his ultimate recovery, touched him greatly. I feel certain that his coming back to this house yesterday was influenced largely by a desire to express to those who had been so kind and had taken such an interest in his well-being his appreciation of their interest in his recovery.
I can say nothing more except this, that we do sincerely appreciate the observations that have been made by the Prime Minister, and we grieve with the devoted wife and family in the loss they have sustained. I should like to join with what my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has said in that regard, for only the day before yesterday I saw sitting beside the doctor's bed his devoted wife. Such relations are indeed an inspiration to every man who sees in them the development of the best in family life which, after all, is the foundation and the strength of all the institutions of our country. Love of wife and family, devotion to the companion of his life and to his children, were strongly manifested in our deceased colleague. It might be said of him, that though dead he still liveth amongst us. While there may be acute differences about many matters, there can be no difference of opinion as to the sincerity of his motives, the singleness of his purpose, the probity of his conduct, the integrity of his character, his great love for home and wife and children, his generous affection for his constituents and kind-hearted regard for his fellow men, his devotion to his country, his love for his empire and respect for this house of which he was so long a member.
We will long mourn him as a faithful and devoted friend whose loyalty was beyond question, whose devotion was beyond cavil, and whose single purpose in life was to serve

The late Hon. J. W. Edwards
his country well and who loved his fellow-men to the fullness of his great heart. I am sure too that we had too little appreciation of the breadth of his vision, the greatness of his intellect, and the power that he wielded throughout this country for the wellbeing of the commonwealth. Perhaps the words of a great poet truly express our sentiment:
He has outsoared the shadow of our night;
Envy and calumny and hate and pain,
And that unrest which men miscall delight,
Can touch him not, and torture him again.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. W. EDWARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last evening at six o'clock we did not anticipate that we would 'be called upon to mourn the loss of one of its prominent members. When we saw Dr. Edwards in the chamber yesterdhy afternoon we all hoped that he had fully recovered from his indisposition of Monday, but unfortunately we are now called upon to mourn his death.
The late Dr. Edwards had taken a very prominent part in the public life of this country for many years past. He was a man of strong convictions, and he was not afraid to voice those convictions on all occasions, and he showed a fearlessness in debate which it would be well for most members of this house also to display.
He was a great humanitarian. Those who had an opportunity of knowing him only slightly became aware of the tremendous interest that he took in the inmates of our penitentiaries, and it was one of his life-long ambitions to see that the men and women who for the time being were restrained of their liberty should be given a better opportunity to become useful members of the community than had been accorded them in the past.
Primarily, on behalf of the prairie provinces, may I express our appreciation of the deep interest which the doctor took in our welfare. We have heard him many times in this house debate the question of the return of our natural resources, and he discussed it on many platforms. I am sure that the western people appreciate very fully the tremendous amount of labour which he expended on our behalf in order to see to it that the western provinces were placed on an equality with the other provinces of the Dominion. I am sure we all regret that he had not lived to see the fruition of his labours.
We in this corner of the house desire to be associated with the remarks of the Prime Minister and of the leader of the opposition in conveying to Mrs. Edwards and to the family our sincere regrets on this occasion.

Can the minister furnish the committee with an estimate of the revenue and expenditure of his department for the year expiring March 31, 1929? The last report which we have is for the year ended March 31, 1928, which report has been printed and distributed. I think the committee would be glad to have the figures, either complete or estimated, for the year just closed.

The returns for the fiscal year 1928-29 have not yet been completed and it would be quite difficult to submit those figures. We may be able to give partial figures up to the 31st of January. However, I will have the matter looked into with a view to submitting all the figures we have. When a quarter is completed it generally takes a couple of months to get in all the returns from outside, compile them and have them ready; my secretary tells me it requires three months. Any information we have I will certainly try to have ready.

When a similar item in the estimate's was being discussed last year the question of wages paid to postal employees was brought to the attention of the committee, and on this occasion I wish again to discuss that question. I believe the wages these employees are receiving run from $90 to $120 a month, and out of this sum there is deducted 5 per cent for superannuation. This is in itself an actual reduction in pay, because in a. great many cases no equivalent is given to the postal employees for the money they pay into the superannuation fund. I believe the Postmaster General has placed on the records of the house certain corespond-ence that passed between himself and the Civil Service Commission, and it was indicated that he was favourable to giving an increase to the postal employees but that the Civil Service Commission stood in the way of the proposal. Somehow or other, while I appreciate the efforts made by the Postmaster General to give to the postal employees an increase in wages such as they are entitled to, and which I believe is endorsed generally by members in all parts of the house, I do not think he has gone quite far enough. I believe that if the government were determined to give to these workers increases in salaries, ways and means could be found to do it. During the past few days there has been done by the government something which in my opinion places the question now in a completely new aspect. I understand that

Supply-Post Office
parliament created the Civil Service Commission for the purpose of determining the salaries and the conditions under which employees of the government should be engaged; and if the government have confidence in the Civil Service Commission then I presume it is quite right and proper for them to accept all the findings of that commission. Within the past few days, however, the Minister of Finance has intimated to parliament the appointment of a special commission which, so far as I can see, is brought into existence for no other reason than that he has no confidence in the findings of the Civil Service Commission. If such is the ease with regard to professional and technical employees of the government, I want to know why the same action should not be taken with regard to the postal employees. If a special commission is to be appointed to investigate the salaries of professional and technical employees, in my opinion there is a thousand times more need to investigate the salaries of men receiving less than $100 a month. The Minister of Finance informs the house that he has appointed three big business men to constitute that commission. My opinion is that the appointment of this commission by the government amounts to a vote of want of confidence in the Civil Service Commission. If the government had confidence in the Civil Service Commission it would not be necessary to appoint a special commission to review their findings; and if the government had no confidence in the findings of the Civil Service Commission with respect to professional and technical employees, I cannot understand how they can have confidence in the commission's findings so far as postal employees are concerned. In spite of the fact that the Postmaster General and members on all sides of the house recognize that the salaries paid postal employees are too low, no action is taken by any responsible minister to appoint a commission to investigate the salaries of these employees. I would offer a suggestion to the Postmaster General. There is certain legislation on the statute books in the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, and I see no reason why the government, having appointed one commission to investigate matters with regard to certain employees, should not put that act into operation and appoint a board representative of the postal employees and the government, with a third party, to investigate salaries in this connection. I do not want to discuss what has been in the past the policy or platform of the Liberal party with regard to employees of the government; that I think is well known to minister themselves, but I do say that, 
living as we do in an era when it is claimed there is so much prosperity in Canada, the employees of the government have a night to expect a decent living wage. No minister of the crown, no member of this house, can stand in his place and claim that $90, or $100, or $110, which is being paid to postal workers, is anything approaching a living wage. Therefore when the salaries of postal workers are under discussion I think the Postmaster General should make an explicit statement as to the attitude of the government and of himself towards these employees.
In reply to the hon gentleman, or rather hon. member-
Gentleman too.

Of course-both. I cannot give any explanation about the appointment of a special commission touching technical officers; that- is not in my line. All I can say is that the postal department has followed as closely as possible the act in its recommendations, where it thought fit, in the matter of increased salaries to postal workers generally throughout the department. There are some technical men in my department, but they come under another class; and so far as I am concerned, as head of the department, I have always felt that wherever it was possible, and wherever deserving, our employees should be paid adequate salaries. But the act fixes a rate, and certain regulations are laid down to be carried out by the Civil Service Commission. When an application is made to them for increases or additional help, which in some oases would mean promotion, the head of the department has nothing whatever to do with the fixing of salaries; it is entirely in the hands of the commission, and as I said before I must, as head of the department, abide by their decision.

Would the Postmaster General tell the house why, when recommendations were made by the commission to the government in the case of technical employees, the government did not accept those recommendations ?

I am not in a position to

Mr. Chairman, at the beginning of this discussion my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) introduced a matter which I consider to be of very great importance. Particular cases were brought up and the attention of the Postmaster General was diverted from this particular matter. The hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) came back to the same question, but before he could get an answer some special cases came up again and attention was again diverted.
I refer to the salaries which are paid to postal workers. It is very generally acknowledged that these salaries are not as high as they should be. This is not a matter which concerns a few individuals, as do the cases which were brought up, however important they may have been, but it is a matter which concerns thousands and tens of thousands of employees of this government. I would suggest further that it is a matter of very great interest to the citizens generally, because there is not a class of civil employees who come into such close contact with the general public as do the postal workers.
There are two aspects of this matter which we should consider. The first is: What are the services of these postal workers worth? I submit that they are doing work of an extremely important and responsible character. There are occasional instances where theft occurs, but I am glad to say that they are only occasional; I wonder that they are not more frequent. I do not say that because a man is being paid a low salary he should yield to temptation, but when a man is en-

gaged in a responsible position he should not be subjected to the temptations to which the low paid postal worker is subjected. These men are required to collect money on their routes; they should be paid with some regard to such responsibilities. Further, there is an immense amount of detail connected with their routine work. We are all accustomed to receiving our letters with great regularity, and it is remarkable how efficient the service is. I submit that the men who are so largely responsible for that efficiency of service are not being paid accordingly.
When the matter is considered from the angle of what is required in order to allow a man to live decently, I think we must admit that these men are not being paid a decent living wage. There are individuals receiving as low as $75 and $80 per month, and large numbers who receive less than $100 per month. I do not think that anyone in this house will say that $100 per month is a living wage for a man with a family to support. A large number of these postal employees are married men, and on account of having a steady position many of them have established homes. They should be paid sufficient salaries to enable them to occupy a decent position in the community.
I have not the statistics at hand, but they have been placed on Hansard again and again and no object would be served by having them placed on Hansard once more. We all know the range of salaries, and we all know how low those salaries are.
I think the member for South Toronto is quite right when he insists that the government should be a model employer. It is not even up to the average. When one considers the responsibilities which are placed upon the ordinary postal workers, the government is much less a model employer. I am afraid that in many instances the low salaries received by the postal workers is apt to lower the general wages paid in the community. I know of particular cases in my own constituency where postal workers have been receiving less than allowances being granted by the charity organizations of the city. A condition like that is nothing less than a disgrace, and should not be allowed to continue -simply because there is no group that has the political strength effectively to demand the rights of these poorly paid workers.
The Post Office department is a self-supporting department, in fact it is the only revenue producing department in connection with the government. WThy, then, should we be niggardly in dealing with the people who are largely responsible for producing this very large revenue? The Postmaster General has
had this called to his attention, again and again, and he tries to hide behind the Civil Sendee Commission. I do not think that is fair. In June, 1923, the parliamentary committee appointed to inquire into the operation of chapter 12, 8 and 9 George V, an act respecting the civil service of Canada, reported as follows:
"Your committee therefore recommends that immediately after reorganization has taken place salary revision and adjustments be proceeded with without delay. Pending this revision the bonus to be continued."
At the commencement of 1924 fiscal year no provision was made for revision of salaries and the bonus, admittedly a necessity under the existing low salary ranges, instead of continuing as recommended was reduced 33 per cent, creating considerable agitation among civil servants generally and the lower grades particularly. The government responded by requesting the Civil Service Commission to revise salaries, commencing with the Post Office Department.
On the completion of such revision it was found that instead of removing the cause of the agitation, namely, loss of remuneration, it aggravated the loss and in a number of instances allowed less remuneration than after the bonus reduction was in operation. Protests from all over the Dominion leading to the dislocation of the postal service in some parts was one result, and the following declaration of the government policy was another:
"The government's policy is that when the Civil Service Commission has submitted its report upon the salaries for the entire civil service that opportunity will be given to the representatives of the employees of the Post Office Department or in other departments of the government who have objections to file against the salary revision proposed by the commission, to fully present their views to a sub-committee of the government and to discuss such matters of differences as fully as may be necessary to insure a thorough understanding, and it is hoped a final and satisfactory agreement on the points in dispute."
That is the quotation of the government's own declaration. Then the letter goes on:
Accordingly representatives of the employees met a sub-committee of the government on June 5, 1925, giving their evidence in writing. The sub-committee of the government did not attempt to come to any agreement, contenting themselves with listening to the evidence submitted and asking questions, subsequently notifying the delegation that no decision could be arrived at till the balance of the civil service had been consulted.
On September 14, 1925, an order in council known as P.C. 1644, wherein the minister recommends that such report be forwarded to the Civil Service Commision with a view to having that body make an upward revision of the salaries in question. Despite frequent appeals of the staff side the report of the revision was not brought before parliament until 1927, allotting a -widely advertised flat rate increase of $120 with certain exceptions, the exceptions being in the majority.
Customs, postal and other employees found themselves in a position, through the manipula-ton between bonuses and salaries, of being told that having received an increase in salary in 1924 of $240 per annum, that they would now only receive $60. No cognizance was apparently taken of the loss of remuneration by bonus abolition, a loss that bore most heavily on those who received the most bonus, the lower paid positions.

One illustration will suffice, and be it understood that though this illustration is taken from the postal service, we could quote others from other departments who are in exactly the same predicament. Section 13 of the Civil Service Act, which will be found in volume 1 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, deals with an entirely different matter altogether. It reads as follows:
The rate of compensation of an employee upon appointment to a position in any class in the civil service shall be at the minimum rate prescribed for the class; provided, however, that when the appointee is already in the civil service in another position, the rate of compensation upon appointment to the new position either through transfer or promotion shall be the same as that received before such appointment or, if there be no such rate for the new class, then at the next higher rate, but no appointment shall in any case be made at less than the minimum or at more than the maximum rate prescribed for a class.
There is no doubt that the Deputy Postmaster General intended to refer to section 24. I presume there has been a re-numbering of the sections and that section 13 in the old act has become section. 24 in the new one. Section 24 reads as follows:
The deputy head may, at any time before the expiration of six months, reject any person
[Mr. Stinson.1
assigned or appointed to any position under his control or direction, or he may extend the period of probation within which such person may be rejected for another six months; and the cause of rejection, or the reason for extending the period of probation, shall be reported by the deputy head to the commission.
This explicitly provides that cause must be assigned for any rejection and reported to the Civil Service Commission. Neither in the letter from the Postmaster General to his deputy, nor in the letter from the deputy to the commission, is any cause assigned for the rejection, and that in spite of the fact that his own inspector had reported on Gerald H. Way as being a fit and proper person and had placed him in the category of merit as No. 1 for the appointment. There is nothing in the opinion of the Justice department, quoted yesterday by the Postmaster General:
If the deputy be reasonably satisfied upon preliminary examination of the person nominated that the latter is unsuitable or not qualified for the duties of the office or employment to which he is assigned,^ I think he may, if he thinks it advisable, reject him without entrusting him with the charge of any duties.
There is nothing in the statute that permits the exercise of any such poweT of rejection as the minister invoked in this case, nor is there anything in the opinion of the Justice department to justify his action, because Gerald H. Way was in charge -of the office -for twenty-three years, and the department's own inspector reports him as a fit and proper person to be appointed. You cannot expect to stop that, but the minister has no right to give way to that pressure in violation of the Civil Service Act. That is what we are complaining about. No deputy head, officer, clerk or employee in the civil service shall be debarred from voting at any Dominion or provincial election if, under the laws governing the said election, he has the right to vote; but no such deputy head, officer, clerk or employee shall engage in partisan work in connection with any such election, or contribute, receive or in any way deal with any money for any party funds.

We have no sympathy with that view at all, or at least I have not. It is not a question here whether the Civil Service Act is to be observed or not. Perhaps I am playing it too much.

There is a very serious principle at stake in connection with the Civil Service Act, and it is this: certain persons secure appointment through competitive examination by the Civil Service Commission. Having passed the examination they are entitled to receive appointment, but there is a reservation, which has a distinct and definite meaning and intent. It appears, I think, in section 13 of the act, if I recall rightly, wherein the minister or the deputy minister is empowered, in the event of an appointee sent over by the Civil Service Commission being incompetent or unsuitable, to call for a second appointment from the commission. And why is that in the act? For this very simple reason. The Civil Service Commission makes its examination-I am not going to go into the details-on certain grounds, allocating certain marks for certain qualifications. There is a verbal examination and a written examination; there is an examination on educational qualifications, and there is an examination on technical qualifications. There is also an examination as to health, intelligence, suitability and so forth. All these things are factors, and it is possible that the commission might choose an individual who by temperament, or by some peculiar physical disability, or for some other reason, might be more or less an irritant in a department; that is to say, an impossible person from the standpoint of temperament. I know of such people myself, who could pass examinations, probably well. It is therefore provided in the statutes that in a case of that kind, an abnormal case, the minister may reject the appointee. But he may not do so for the purpose of appointing his own choice; he may not defeat the
[Mr. Stevens. 1
purpose of the act. He can ask the Civil Service Commission to make a second appointment. Now why does the minister persist in the course he has followed? Take the case referred to by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) to-night. A young lady tries the examination; she seeks to enter the civil service as a life work. She passes her examination, receives notice from the commission that she is appointed, resigns her present position, and goes and reports for duty as she is instructed to do by the government of Canada. Can we expect private citizens to understand not only all the intricacies of the statutes of the land, but all the idiosyncrascies of the minister? Can we expect it? Not very well. They act on good faith, believing that when they receive a document signed by a government official the Dominion government is behind that document. So this young lady resigned her job and reported for duty. They dilly-dallied for a month, and then she was coolly told that the Post Office department had not ratified her appointment. And in her place was put a young man, a boy in fact-under the civil service age by the way-who was the son of a very prominent supporter of my hon. friend; not that he is any the worse for that, but it is a rather significant coincidence. It is the same in case after case, incident after incident. The Civil Service Commission's recommendation is repudiated by the minister and a particular friend substituted.
Now the country asks the government, the country is expecting of parliament, a vindication of the Civil Service Act. That is what the country is asking for-a vindication of the act. And we intend, so far as we are concerned, to insist that the facts be brought out. I am inviting the government, as I did this afternoon and do again to-night-not the Postmaster General, because that I conceive to be hopeless, but I do invite the government as a whole-seriously to take this matter up. They can do it in conclave if they like, but let them take it up and tell the house whether or not the Civil Service Act is to be a joke, whether it is to be defied, or whether we are going to pay at least reasonable respect to its provisions. You will please make arrangements for the removal of the postmaster at North Brookfield. Queens County, N.S., and appoint in his stead Mr. Nelson Frank of that place.

I will bring down the information if it is not on a private file. I have stated that before and I will go no farther.
I have a right to adhere to that practice, because it has been the practice of the house not to produce any documents on the ministers' private files, which are marked "personal". I am not going to be driven to take that action in this case.

I assume that it was upon
the recommendation of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) that this dismissal took place, but can a member have a public servant of this country dismissed and have his letter treated as sacred by simply marking it "personal"? If that is the practice of the Post Office Department, there is something radically wrong. If a member wanted a particular action taken by any minister of the crown, all he would have to do would be to put "personal" across his letter and the minister could say, "This is on my private file and I will not produce it." That is the stand which has been taken by the Postmaster General. I ask the members of the house: When a public servant is dismissed should not the reason be given to the house; have we not the right to know? We are here representing the people. I am here representing the constituency of Queens-Lunenburg, and the people of my constituency want to know why this action was taken.

Mr. Chairman, as I have said before this evening, if this house desires to pass supply it can not be passed on that statement. We owe a duty to the public which is of far more importance. I hope the house realizes what is involved in this, and as it is near eleven o'clock the Postmaster General will have an opportunity before supply is next moved to consider whether or not a letter, upon which a public official is dismissed, can be marked "personal", and therefore not brought down to the house. That is the question at issue. Supply has been withheld in other countries for less reason than that, and I feel perfectly certain that on mature consideration the government will not take that position. Remember that governments do not endure forever, and it is establishing a precedent.
The shadow government had its day.

I should say that there is one member who should be very thankful for that because it enabled him to become a member of this parliament for a short time.
If it were not so serious we would not take up the time of the house discussing the matter, but, as I say, governments do not last forever and our position to-day may be

the position of my hon. friends opposite some other day. When the Postmaster General said that this principle was applied in the past, he was speaking of an entirely different matter. A personal letter written to a min. ister about a personal matter and placed upon his personal file is privileged, and this house has so ruled. But a letter marked "personal" which deals with the public business of Canada cannot be made personal merely by marking it so. That principle has been laid down by parliament from the first time the production of papers was called for, because parliament claims the right to redress grievances and it claims the right to know what the grievances are before supply is granted. The only time this matter can be placed before parliament is when supply is being sought. It would be an intolerable thing if all you had to do was to mark communications to a minister "personal" and know that they could not be brought down as part of the file. I do not think there is a minister in this country except the Postmaster General who would suggest that that be done. The rules to which he referred are rules which deal purely with personal communications. For instance, if I write a letter to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and say that I hope he is enjoying better health and I very much regret that he has been laid up for so long a period, his secretary, if he keeps it at all and does not send it to the waste paper basket, puts it upon the personal file and that is the end of it. But if I say to the minister in that letter, "I strongly recommend that John Smith be appointed a judge of the county court. He has qualifications of a very peculiar character and they should not be overlooked-"
And the man is appointed.
I do not think he would be appointed upon my recommendation.

He might write to the
